title: Investment Fees
summary: FIND THE MER → COMPARE → SWITCH IF IT’S WORTH IT
subtitle: Check your investment statement for a line called fees. You probably won’t find one. That’s not because your investments are free.

blocks.text: Check your investment statement. Look for a line called “fees.” You probably won’t find one.

That’s not because your investments are free. Most investment fees in Canada are built into the product, taken out before you see a return. No withdrawal from your account. No invoice. Just a slightly smaller number, every day, that you never saw being taken.
This lesson is about finding that hidden number, and seeing how much it matters.
Find the hidden fee in your investments and keep more of your own growth.
blocks.detail: A few minutes of checking can save you thousands a year and six figures over a lifetime.
blocks.extra: Section 04 shows how a small fee grows into a huge gap.

sections.title: The MER: the number that matters most

blocks.text: Almost every fund, mutual fund or ETF, charges a Management Expense Ratio, or MER. It’s a yearly percentage of your investment, taken automatically, whether the fund goes up or down that year.

A 1% MER on a $50,000 investment costs $500 a year. A 2% MER on the same amount costs $1,000. That doesn’t feel like much in one year. Over decades, it becomes one of the biggest costs of your financial life.
Here’s why it’s so easy to miss. The MER isn’t taken out as a withdrawal you can see. It’s built into the fund’s daily returns. You just earn a little less than the fund made, every day you own it.

items.title: “If I’m not paying a visible fee, my investments must be free to hold.”
items.text: Almost nothing in investing is free. The MER comes out of the fund’s returns before you see them, which is why it feels invisible. Look for it on your fund’s fact sheet. It’s disclosed, just not obvious.

sections.title: Mutual funds and ETFs: a real gap, not a small one

blocks.text: Both hold similar things: stocks, bonds or a mix. But the fee difference between them, on average, is large.
Typical yearly fees
blocks.detail: MER, as a share of your balance

items.title: Bank-sold mutual funds
items.text: Around 1.5% to 2% — often including a fee paid to the seller.

items.title: Broad-market index ETFs
items.text: 0.05% to 0.25% — for a fund that tracks a whole market.

items.title: All-in-one balanced ETFs
items.text: Around 0.20% to 0.25% — for a full mix of stocks and bonds in one fund.

blocks.text: On a $100,000 portfolio, a 0.20% ETF costs about $200 a year. A 2% mutual fund costs about $2,000 a year on the same balance. Same money invested, ten times the yearly cost.

sections.title: Why a 1.5% gap becomes a six-figure gap

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHY A 1.5% GAP BECOMES A SIX-FIGURE GAP

A fee gap that looks small in one year grows into something huge over a working life, and almost nobody feels it happening. The fee doesn’t just cost you the fee. It also costs the growth that money would have earned every year after, compounding alongside your investments. Here’s an example: $200,000 held for 25 years, with the investments earning 6% a year before fees. At a 0.20% fee, it grows to about $820,000. At a 2% fee, it grows to about $533,000. That’s a gap of nearly $290,000, from a fee you never saw on a bill. This is the most important number in this lesson. Fees don’t just cost you the fee. They cost you what the fee would have grown into.

sections.title: What’s actually bundled inside that percentage

blocks.text: The MER isn’t one single charge. It bundles several things together.

items.title: The management fee. Paid to whoever runs the fund and makes the buy and sell decisions.
Operating costs. Administration, legal costs and audits: the overhead of running the fund.
A trailing commission, in many bank-sold mutual funds. Often 0.5% to 1% a year, paid to whoever sold you the fund, whether or not they ever call you again.

blocks.text: That last one surprises people most. It isn’t a one-time sales fee. It’s a yearly payment, built into your MER, that keeps going as long as you hold the fund, whether or not you get any advice in return. Since June 2022, discount brokers, which give no advice, can no longer be paid trailing commissions, and funds can no longer charge a fee for selling early (a deferred sales charge).

items.title: “A higher MER usually means better investment performance.”
items.text: There’s no reliable evidence of this, and plenty showing the opposite. A higher fee is a sure cost. Better performance is never sure. Paying more doesn’t reliably buy you more. It just reliably costs you more.

blocks.text: Since 2016, your annual statement has shown some fees in dollars, mainly what you paid your dealer, including trailing commissions. But it left out the biggest cost: the fund’s own MER. New rules fix that. Starting with the 2026 year, your annual report must show the total dollar cost of your funds, MER included. The first of these reports arrive in early 2027.
Until then, every fund has a fact sheet, usually a page or two, with the MER near the top. Search your fund’s name plus “fact sheet” or “MER,” and it will usually turn up in seconds.
Checking your own investment costs

items.title: I know the MER on every fund I currently hold, not just a rough guess.
I’ve checked my annual statement for the dollar fees I paid, and I’ll look for the full cost report in 2027.
If I hold a bank-sold mutual fund, I’ve checked whether it includes a trailing commission.
I’ve compared my fund’s MER to a comparable low-cost ETF in the same category.
I understand that a higher fee is a guaranteed cost, not a guarantee of better performance.

blocks.text: Grant’s twenty-minute phone call
paragraphs: Grant ran a small bakery in Moncton. Eleven years earlier, the week he opened his first bank account, an adviser at the branch had set him up in a mutual fund. He had added to it every month since and never looked at the fee. It wasn’t a number that appeared anywhere obvious.
One night, over a beer, his friend Nadia asked what MER he was paying. Grant shrugged. He had no idea. Nadia raised an eyebrow, and the question stuck with him all the next day.

That afternoon, between batches of bread, he called his bank. The fund’s MER was 2.1%. On his balance of $90,000, that was close to $1,900 a year, paid without a bill or a withdrawal he could ever see.

His first instinct was to sell everything that night and move it all. But he made himself slow down. He spent a weekend comparing low-cost options and asked the bank what, if anything, he was getting for that 2.1%. The answer was a yearly phone call he usually missed.

He also checked one thing Nadia had warned him about. His fund was inside an RRSP, so switching wouldn’t trigger any tax. He moved his savings into an all-in-one ETF with an MER of about 0.25%, saving roughly $1,650 a year on the same balance.
Grant still bakes bread at 4 a.m. Now, every January, he spends twenty minutes on one more job: checking what his investments cost him, before he checks what they earned.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: SWITCHING FUNDS DOES NOT ALWAYS MEAN A TAX BILL

Grant’s move was simple for one reason: his fund was inside a registered account. Sell one fund and buy another inside an RRSP, TFSA, RESP, FHSA or RDSP, and the swap isn’t taxed. Nothing inside those accounts is taxed until money comes out, and for a TFSA or a qualifying FHSA withdrawal, not even then. The tax question only comes up in a non-registered account, where selling a fund that has grown can trigger capital gains tax. Check that before you switch anything held outside a registered account. Before switching any fund, also ask whether there’s a fee for selling, and whether you’re giving up advice you value.

Investment fees are almost always hidden, taken from returns before you see them. The MER is the number to find, and the gap between a typical mutual fund and a low-cost ETF can grow into six figures over a working life. Check your own fund’s MER. A higher fee is a sure cost, never a sure benefit.
One phone call about fees can be worth more than any stock tip.
blocks.detail: Knowing your MER lets you decide whether what you pay matches what you get.
blocks.extra: Section 08 walks you through your own fee check.

items.title: Find the MER on every fund you hold. Check the fact sheet or ask directly. Don’t estimate.
Check your annual statement for the dollar fees you paid. From 2027, look for the new report that includes your funds’ MER in dollars.
If your MER is well above 1%, look up a similar lower-cost option and ask your adviser or bank why the difference exists.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your fee check

Answer guidance: if you don’t know your MERs, that’s this week’s task. Nothing else in this lesson matters until you know your own numbers. If you find a big gap, have a real conversation before you decide. Understand what you might give up, such as advice, service or a specific strategy, before you switch.

items.title: MER
items.text: Management Expense Ratio. A fund’s yearly fee, as a percentage, taken automatically from its returns.

items.title: Trailing commission
items.text: A yearly payment, built into a mutual fund’s MER, paid to whoever sold you the fund.

items.title: CRM2
items.text: Rules from 2016 that made statements show some fees in dollars. Full fund costs are added from the 2026 year.

items.title: Asset-weighted average
items.text: An average that counts how much money sits in each fund, not just the number of funds.

blocks.text: Educational only, not investment advice. Fee ranges are typical, not exact. Check your own fund’s fee before assuming anything.

quiz.question: True or False: “If I’m not paying a visible fee, my investments must be free to hold.”

questions: Which funds do you hold, and what is each one’s MER?
What dollar fees did your last annual statement show?
Do any of your funds pay a trailing commission?
Roughly what would a similar low-cost ETF charge on the same balance?
Are your funds inside a registered account, or outside one?
What will you ask your bank or adviser about your fees?
